implementation_notes: Rust deliberately has no runtime trait-implementation test: the standard library states that `&dyn Any` 'is limited to testing whether a value is of a specified concrete type, and cannot be used to test whether a type implements a trait'. The runtime query is therefore either a concrete-type test - keep the value as `&dyn Any`/`Box<dyn Any>` and call downcast_ref::<T>(), which yields Some(&T) only for exactly that type and only for 'static values - or a capability the trait itself declares (the second variant: an accessor returning Option<&dyn Capability>). What replaces the classic structure is the compile-time route: a generic parameter or where-clause makes the capability a precondition the compiler proves, so the runtime question is reserved for genuinely dynamic boundaries. Trait upcasting to `&dyn Any` (Rust 1.86) removed the as_any() bridge this form used to require.
pitfalls: Any requires 'static: a type that borrows non-'static data cannot be queried through downcast_ref, and TypeId::of is likewise only available for 'static types.

downcast_ref matches one exact concrete type - it cannot discover that a value implements a capability trait, so shared behaviour must be expressed as an explicit accessor (second variant) or as an enum.

The dyn Any route erases Send/Sync: a Box<dyn Any> query loses the auto-trait information the sender had, so a capability that must cross threads needs the bridge written as &(dyn Any + Send + Sync) (the as_any idiom) rather than an assumption that the query preserves it.
A TypeId- or Any-keyed extension map answers about types rather than capabilities: two implementations of the same capability are different keys and neither is a general answer.

variants.name: Declared capability accessor (Option<&dyn Cap>)
variants.implementation_notes: The trait-based realisation makes the object answer the question itself: the base trait declares an accessor with a default None, and implementers that have the capability override it with Some(self). This is the runtime analogue Rust APIs actually use for optional trait support (the pattern behind as_any(), and the same shape as a coercion to a capability trait object); it keeps the capability list open for downstream implementers, unlike an enum, and needs no TypeId registry or 'static bound. Choose it when the queried object is already a trait object and the capability is itself a trait; keep dyn Any downcasting for concrete payload types such as plugin state.
variants.idiom_name: fn as_flushable(&self) -> Option<&dyn Flushable> with a default None
pitfalls: A default accessor returning None means a new capability needs a new trait method: the capability set is fixed where the base trait is defined, so plan the accessor set or accept that adding capabilities is an additive API change to a public trait.
Every implementer must remember to override the accessor; forgetting it yields a silent 'no' rather than a compile error, so the accessor belongs in the trait's documented contract.
The accessor can be called in hot loops, and the returned &dyn Capability borrows from the object - cache the handle, and mind that it keeps the object borrowed for the handle's lifetime.
